q: How are stamps printed?
What is intaglio printing for stamps?
What is lithography in stamp printing?
What is photogravure in stamp production?
What is letterpress stamp printing?
What are the different stamp printing methods?
What is recess printing?
What is typography printing for stamps?
a: Stamp printing methods have evolved significantly since the first postage stamps of 1840, and identifying the printing method is often critical for distinguishing similar stamps of different values. Intaglio (also called recess or engraved printing) is the oldest and most prestigious method, where the design is engraved into a metal plate, ink fills the recessed lines, and high-pressure presses transfer the design onto paper, producing stamps with sharp, raised detail that is difficult to counterfeit—features include a slightly embossed feel and rich, permanent colors. Lithography (offset and photolithography) uses a flat plate where the design area attracts ink and non-design area repels it via chemical treatment, offering excellent detail for multicolor designs with lower production costs. Photogravure uses acid-etched cells of varying depth on a copper cylinder to produce continuous-tone images ideal for photographic reproductions, while typography (letterpress) prints from a raised surface like a rubber stamp, producing visible ink indentation on the back of the stamp. Many modern stamps combine multiple methods—bicolor intaglio with photogravure backgrounds—and the printing method is often listed in stamp catalogs as a key distinguishing feature between similar issues.

q: How are stamp papers made?
What is laid paper vs wove paper in stamps?
What is chalky paper in stamps?
What is granite paper?
What is security paper for stamps?
What are phosphorescent tags on stamps?
What is stamp paper composition?
What is the difference between stamp paper types?
a: Stamp paper is specially manufactured to meet security, durability, and printing requirements distinct from ordinary paper, with composition varying from rag (cotton fiber) papers used in early issues to modern wood-pulp and synthetic fiber blends. Paper types include wove (the most common, with a uniform texture showing no visible mesh lines), laid (showing alternating thick and thin translucent lines from the paper mold), batonne (widely spaced laid lines), quadrillé (grid pattern), ribbed (corrugated texture), granite (containing dyed fibers visible to the naked eye as a security feature), and chalky paper (coated with a chalk or clay surface that prevents reuse because the ink soaks in and the stamp self-destructs if soaking is attempted). Modern stamps increasingly incorporate security features into the paper itself, including fluorescent fibers (visible under UV light), phosphorescent tagging bands (used for automatic mail sorting to detect stamp presence and orientation), micro-perforations, iridescent strips, hidden images, and chemical markers that enable postal automation while making forgery more difficult.

q: What are stamp printing errors?
What are inverted centers on stamps?
What are color errors on stamps?
What are perforation errors?
What are missing color stamps?
What are the most famous stamp errors?
What makes a stamp error valuable?
What are plate varieties on stamps?
a: Stamp printing errors are among the most valuable and sought-after philatelic items, occurring when something goes wrong during the printing, perforation, or production process. Major error types include inverted centers (the central design element is printed upside-down relative to the frame, such as the famous 1918 US 24-cent Inverted Jenny airmail stamp, one of the world's most famous errors), color omissions (one or more colors missing from a multicolor design), color shifts (colors printed out of registration), perforation errors (imperforate between stamps, double perforations, or perforations missing entirely on one side), and paper errors (wrong paper type used accidentally). The value of an error depends on its visual appeal, how dramatic the mistake is, the scarcity of the error versus the normal stamp, and the stamp's overall desirability—the 1855 Sweden 3-skilling Banco color error (printed on yellow paper instead of the correct green) is the most valuable stamp in the world, with a single unused copy selling for millions of dollars.
